hints: Focus on whether a new insoluble solid is actually formed, not just whether a solid was added at the start.
Recall that Group 2 hydroxides get more soluble down the group, so calcium hydroxide is sparingly soluble while barium hydroxide is soluble, and that barium sulfate is famously insoluble.
Check each test-tube for a precipitation or sparingly soluble product, then count only those that leave a white solid at the end.
walkthrough:
**Recall what counts as a white solid product**

A white solid product means a precipitate or sparingly soluble compound formed by the reaction. A starting solid that simply dissolves, or an excess reactant left over, does not count unless a new solid is made.

Rule to use:
$$\text{insoluble product} = \text{white precipitate (s)}$$

**Test-tube 1: Calcium + water**

Calcium is reactive and forms calcium hydroxide, which is sparingly soluble and appears white and milky.

$$\text{Ca(s)} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2\text{(s/aq)} + \text{H}_2\text{(g)}$$ 
So this mixture does produce a white solid.

**Test-tube 2 and Test-tube 3: No precipitate**

For barium chloride + strontium hydroxide, the possible swap gives barium hydroxide and strontium chloride, both of which are soluble in water, so no solid forms.

$$\text{BaCl}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{Sr(OH)}_2\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{SrCl}_2\text{(aq)}$$ 
For calcium carbonate + excess acid, the solid carbonate reacts to give soluble calcium chloride plus gas and water, so the white solid disappears.

$$\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)} + 2\text{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2\text{(aq)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$$

**Test-tube 4: Classic sulfate test**

Magnesium sulfate + barium nitrate swaps to give barium sulfate, which is insoluble and white, plus soluble magnesium nitrate.

$$\text{MgSO}_4\text{(aq)} + \text{Ba(NO}_3)_2\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4\text{(s)} + \text{Mg(NO}_3)_2\text{(aq)}$$ 
So this mixture does produce a white solid. Counting tube 1 and tube 4 gives 2 mixtures in total.

options.A: 0 is too low because two reactions clearly make an insoluble white solid: sparingly soluble calcium hydroxide in tube 1 and insoluble barium sulfate in tube 4.
options.B: 1 is incorrect because students often remember only the famous barium sulfate precipitate and forget that calcium hydroxide from Ca + water is sparingly soluble and gives a white milky solid.
options.C: 2 is correct. Tube 1 gives white sparingly soluble Ca(OH)2 and tube 4 gives white insoluble BaSO4. Tubes 2 and 3 give only soluble aqueous products, so no solid remains.
options.D: 3 is incorrect because it counts one extra. Tube 2 gives all soluble products and tube 3 dissolves the CaCO3 solid to soluble CaCl2, so neither can add to the count.
